summary:
We found places on Earth that are like the Moon and Mars, so scientists can practice there before building real bases. We used NASA data to compare five lesser-known sites: Jingpo Lake (China), Mistastin Lake (Canada), Dalangtan Playa (China), Lonar Crater (India) and Miyake-jima (Japan). We ranked them and showed what each one copies well and what it doesn't.

This answers the challenge by looking beyond famous sites and using real evidence. It matters because astronauts and rovers need good places to practice, and no place on Earth is a perfect copy of the Moon or Mars.
details:
Project details

What does it do, and how does it work?

It finds places on Earth that can be practice grounds for future Moon and Mars bases. We collected real NASA measurements for the Moon and Mars, searched for lesser-known sites, compared each one with that data, and ranked the best five.

What benefits does it have?

It shows which site copies which part of the Moon or Mars, so teams can pick the right place for the right test. It also points to overlooked sites and states each site's limits.

What is the intended impact?

To help scientists choose test sites for rovers and astronaut training, and to encourage research at under-studied places like Jingpo Lake (China) and Miyake-jima (Japan).

What tools did you use?

We used NASA's official website and published scientific papers as our main sources. We used AI tools to ask questions, check information and verify facts against those sources. We made the presentation of our ideas in Canva. No coding was used; this is a research-based project.

How is it creative?

We chose lesser-known sites instead of the famous ones, and added a Moon-crystal site (Miyake-jima).

What factors did your team consider?

Quality of evidence, measured conditions (gravity, air, temperature, radiation, rocks, landforms), usefulness for a base, and novelty. We also showed the limits: no Earth site matches the Moon's or Mars's gravity, air or radiation.
